text: VO: With the explosive growth of massive data centers in states like Virginia, many Americans are convinced that artificial intelligence, and the infrastructure needed to run it, are what’s to blame for rising electric bills. While Idaho doesn’t have the development incentives to the same level Virgina does, it’s still an appealing location to build a new data center – both for the relatively low cost of electricity, and for the state’s friendly business climate. JIM Buie: ‘The reliability, predictability, and just the pragmatic business climate. | Idaho checks those boxes from a business perspective. It happens to have favorable environmental conditions as well.’ VO: Data center company Valor C3 provides services to mid-tier businesses that have outgrown an internal server room but don’t need a full data facility of their own. CEO Jim Buie said Valor C3 appreciates the community just as much as – if not more than – the low cost of power. Why are we having to pay more all of a sudden. VO: Idaho Power is proud of the fact that its rates are competitive, especially compared to other parts of the nation. Executive Vice President Adam Richins told Idaho Reports that reliable service, and keeping rates from rising too quickly, are the power company’s top priorities. Richins: ‘We have kept it at about 1.2% which we don’t love but still better than others.’ VO: But local power bills are still rising, which has customers worried. with inflation, and that has implications for the future. Richins: “This last year we did have a rate increase, it ended up being settled at about 7% so that maybe what some folks are talking about. That rate case did not have any dollars related to large load infrastructure because they pay for that all upfront” Richins: “Idaho has been very strict on this mantra of growth pays for growth. So if you’re going to come for our service territory, that’s great. We have really low rates. You need to pay your way to make sure those costs aren’t spread to other customers. VO: Public utilities like Idaho Power operate as regulated monopolies under the Public Utilities Commission, which reviews utility contracts and agreements in a mostly public fashion. Richins: It’s a public process. Any party that wants to intervene that has representation can intervene. So then they propose increases based on that. Richins: “So it’s not necessarily the irrigators or… of what the rates should be.” VO: Lawmakers continued negotiations this year, DEBATING whether to regulate large loads (like data centers) more strictly than the existing PUC (say “Public Utilities Commission” again close to end?) process. It’s been really successful so far | Our rates are the lowest in the nation in Idaho. These processes has been a part of that so let's keep them in place and rely on them as we move forward.” VO: [House Bill 911 (2026)] --- THE VOID ___ VO: Rather than create an entirely parallel review process or tie the hands of the Public Utilities Commission, the Senate proposed codifying current practices. The House wants a no-harm test as part of the process, requiring the PUC to consider whether existing customers’ bills and service reliability will stay the as they would have without the new large load user. VO: The House overwhelmingly passed a compromise bill two weeks ago, which splits the difference between the other bills. If passed in to law, the Public Utilities Commission would review new large load service contracts – defined at the widest threshold yet in this bill, a facility using 50MW over 5 years – to ensure the public utility is reasonably expected to maintain existing service, and that the new load is responsible for its full cost of service.
